references.text: The Lord warns that he will send very heavy hail, the likes of which have never been seen in Egypt since the land was founded.
The locust plague is also described as without parallel in Egyptian history, using similar language to that used for the hail plague.
The final plague is also described as without precedent, with the same wording that nothing like this has ever happened before in Egypt.
The psalm describes how God destroyed the Egyptians' vines with hail and their sycamore trees with frost, and gave their livestock over to the hail.
The psalm mentions that God gave the Egyptians hail instead of rain, and flaming fire in their land.
Isaiah describes the Lord's judgment with hailstorms and consuming fire, similar to the images from the plague in Egypt.
Ezekiel describes God's judgment with pestilence, blood, torrential rain, hailstones, fire, and sulfur.
Revelation describes hail and fire mixed with blood being thrown on the earth, which recalls the plague in Egypt.
Great hail, each stone weighing a talent, falls from heaven upon people, an eschatological parallel to Egypt's hail plague.
A theological parallel showing how the historical judgment against Egypt foreshadows the final judgment on the earth in Revelation.
A poetic allusion to the Exodus plague that illustrates God's divine power and judgment in a context of praise.
